segments.text: How can a poll of just one thousand people predict an election?
segments.caption: How can a poll of just 1,000 people predict an election?

segments.text: The Central Limit Theorem. One example in detail, then four more places it's used. Save this one!
segments.caption: The Central Limit Theorem. One example in detail, then 4 more places it's used. Save this one!

segments.text: Millions of people will vote. A pollster can't ask them all, so they ask one thousand random voters.
segments.caption: Millions of people will vote. A pollster can't ask them all, so they ask 1,000 random voters.

segments.text: Each person gives one answer: yes or no. As data, that's just two bars. Nothing like a bell curve.
segments.caption: Each person gives one answer: yes or no. As data, that's just two bars. Nothing like a bell curve.

segments.text: Now count the yeses: five hundred and twenty out of a thousand. That's fifty-two percent.
segments.caption: Now count the yeses: 520 out of 1,000. That's 52%.

segments.text: And here's the key. Every yes is a one, every no is a zero. Fifty-two percent is just their average.
segments.caption: And here's the key. Every yes is a 1, every no is a 0. 52% is just their average.

segments.text: Now imagine running the same poll again and again, each time with a different thousand people.
segments.caption: Now imagine running the same poll again and again, each time with a different 1,000 people.

segments.text: You'd get fifty-one, then fifty-three, fifty-two, fifty, fifty-four. Stack all those results, and they form a bell curve.
segments.caption: You'd get 51, then 53, 52, 50, 54. Stack all those results, and they form a bell curve.

segments.text: Most results land close to the middle. Only a few land far away.
segments.caption: Most results land close to the middle. Only a few land far away.

segments.text: That's the Central Limit Theorem: averages form a bell, even when each answer is just yes or no.
segments.caption: That's the Central Limit Theorem: averages form a bell, even when each answer is just yes or no.

segments.text: How wide is that bell? Its spread, the standard error, is the square root of p times one minus p, over n.
segments.caption: How wide is that bell? Its spread, the standard error, is the square root of p times 1 - p, over n.

segments.text: Point five two times point four eight, over a thousand, square-rooted: about one point six percent.
segments.caption: 0.52 × 0.48, over 1,000, square-rooted: about 1.6%.

segments.text: In a bell, ninety-five percent of results land within about two standard errors. Two times one point six: about three percent.
segments.caption: In a bell, 95% of results land within about 2 standard errors. 2 × 1.6: about 3%.

segments.text: So the pollster can say: fifty-two percent, plus or minus three. The true support is probably between forty-nine and fifty-five.
segments.caption: So the pollster can say: 52%, ±3%. The true support is probably between 49 and 55.

segments.text: That range, forty-nine to fifty-five, is the margin of error, also called a ninety-five percent confidence interval.
segments.caption: That range, 49 to 55, is the margin of error, also called a 95% confidence interval.

segments.text: Without the Central Limit Theorem, there would be no plus or minus at all.
segments.caption: Without the Central Limit Theorem, there would be no plus or minus at all.

segments.text: Want a smaller margin? Ask four times as many people. Four thousand voters halves it, to plus or minus one and a half.
segments.caption: Want a smaller margin? Ask 4 times as many people. 4,000 voters halves it, to ±1.5%.

segments.caption: A/B tests: the average spend per user, compared between two versions.

segments.text: Factories: the average weight of five bottles, checked every hour.
segments.caption: Factories: the average weight of 5 bottles, checked every hour.

segments.text: Insurance: the average claim of thousands of customers, used to set premiums.
segments.caption: Insurance: the average claim of thousands of customers, used to set premiums.

segments.text: And machine learning: test accuracy, which is an average of right and wrong predictions.
segments.caption: And machine learning: test accuracy, which is an average of right and wrong predictions.

segments.text: Same idea every time: single values can be messy, but averages form a bell, and the bell tells you how sure to be.
segments.caption: Same idea every time: single values can be messy, but averages form a bell, and the bell tells you how sure to be.
